[BURSEVI:v8p245#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Al-Hamid means the one who alone deserves praise for this and all other acts.
[BURSEVI:v8p245#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · بعضهم | reports | Another view makes al-Wali the controller who repeatedly sends rain, and al-Hamid the praiseworthy one: wise rain reveals need, strengthens resolve, and God answers the distressed.
[BURSEVI:v8p245#2/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · عمر | reports | During severe drought and public despair, Umar said that it must mean rain had come, alluding to this verse.
[BURSEVI:v8p245#2/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · المثنوي | reports | The Mathnawi depicts calamity as prompting supplication and intercession, followed by God’s address that He has given them drink.
[BURSEVI:v8p245#2/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas reports a sea beneath the Throne supplying animal provisions by divine command; rain descends heaven to heaven, is strained, and each measured drop is placed by an angel, except the unmeasured Flood.
[BURSEVI:v8p245/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Al-ghayth is rain that relieves people from drought, specifically beneficial rain, since rain can harm or come at the wrong time.
[BURSEVI:v8p245/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الراغب | reports | Al-Raghib distinguishes الغيث, used for rain, from الغوث, used for aid.
[BURSEVI:v8p245/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Mentioning rain after despair recalls the fullness of the blessing: relief after hopelessness and hardship brings greater joy and prompts gratitude, although rain also comes at other times.
[BURSEVI:v8p245/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | ينشر means to spread or scatter.
[ALUSI-FULL:v25p39/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Ghayth is rain that brings relief from drought and is beneficial; not every kind of rain is called ghayth.
[ALUSI-FULL:v25p39/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الجمهور | reports | The majority read yunazzilu with a light consonant, without doubling.
[ALUSI-FULL:v25p39/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Mentioning that the rain comes after people despair of it recalls God's favor, though the rain also descends at other times.
[ALUSI-FULL:v25p39/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الأعمش وابن وثاب | reports | Al-Aʿmash and Ibn Waththab read qanitu with kasra on the nūn.
[ALUSI-FULL:v25p39/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | God spreads the rain's benefits and effects through plains, mountains, plants, and animals; alternatively, this refers broadly to His encompassing mercy, of which those are a primary instance.
[ALUSI-FULL:v25p39/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · المهدوي | reports | Al-Mahdawi says the mercy is the sun appearing after prolonged rain has wearied people; the author rejects this as unsound.
[ALUSI-FULL:v25p39/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · السدي | rejects | Al-Suddi identifies the mercy as the rain itself, which the author calls very far-fetched because it repeats the same blessing in two expressions.
[ALUSI-FULL:v25p39/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The pronoun in His mercy refers to God; under the first interpretation of mercy's spread, it may instead refer to the rain.
[ALUSI-FULL:v25p39/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Wali is the one who benevolently tends His servants and spreads mercy; al-Hamid is the one alone deserving praise for this.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p124/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | A Qur’an commentator should learn the recurring conventions of Qur’anic wording and arrangement; some early authorities identified such patterns.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p124/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says every Qur’anic occurrence of “ka’s” means wine; al-Tabari also transmits this convention from al-Dahhak.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p124/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · ابن عيينة | reports | Sufyan ibn Uyayna says the Qur’an uses “rain” (maṭar) only for punishment, while Arabs call rain “ghayth,” as in this verse.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p124/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says Qur’anic addresses beginning “O people” refer to the Meccan polytheists.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p124/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الجاحظ | reports | Al-Jahiz notes recurring paired concepts in the Qur’an: prayer and almsgiving, hunger and fear, paradise and hell, hope and dread, emigrants and helpers, and jinn and humans.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p124/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ibn Ashur adds benefit and harm, and heaven and earth, to al-Jahiz’s examples of paired Qur’anic concepts.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p23#4/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · مقاتل | reports | Muqatil excludes the passage from verse 23 through verse 24 from the otherwise Meccan surah; it is said to have been revealed about the Ansar and is among Ibn Abbas's four cited verses. | mentions 42:23, 42:24
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p23#4/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | God owns the heavens and earth, whose realms submit to Him; as creator of beings, He chooses messengers and may legislate for this community as for earlier ones.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p23#4/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | All messengers sent to address people generally were human recipients of revelation; God had not previously sent angels to address the masses directly.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p23#4/r12] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The polytheists have no proof beyond imitating leaders of disbelief who instituted idolatry and planted doubts among them.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p23#4/r13] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The surah warns of Judgment and the approaching Hour, describing idolaters' punishment while alluding to believers' honor.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p23#4/r14] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Reflection shows that the Prophet does not invent claims about God, since God would not allow him to attribute words falsely to Him.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p23#4/r15] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The surah presents signs of divine unity, including blessings such as navigation at sea and worldly provisions.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p23#4/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · مقاتل | reports | Muqatil also says the passage in verses 39–41 about responding to aggression was revealed in Medina. | mentions 42:39, 42:40, 42:41
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p23#4/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الجعبري عن جابر بن زيد | reports | In the order attributed by al-Jaʿbari from Jabir ibn Zayd, the surah followed al-Kahf and preceded Ibrahim, and was the sixty-ninth revealed.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p23#4/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · مقاتل | reports | Muqatil says verse 28 was revealed when rain stopped in Mecca; if so, the surah's revelation began around year eight and may have continued into year nine.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p23#4/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | Ibn ʿAshur suggests revelation may have continued into year nine, after the Aqaba pledge, because the Ansar could be intended in verse 38 even before the Hijra. | mentions 42:38
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p23#4/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Madinan, Meccan, Syrian, and Basran verse counts give the surah fifty verses, while the Kufan count gives fifty-three.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p23#4/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The surah challenges those who deny revelation to produce speech like the Quran, a challenge common to surahs opened by disjointed letters, as in al-Baqara. | mentions 2:1
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p23#4/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | God argue
<<part 2 ends; continues in part 3>>

<<42:28 notes, part 3 of 0..3>>
s that Muhammad's revelation resembles that given to earlier messengers and warns Mecca and its surroundings of Judgment.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p93/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Rain is singled out as a universally acknowledged blessing, foundational to life because it produces good food for people and animals; this prepares for the following sign of living creatures. | mentions 42:29
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p93/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The rain verse is joined to measured provision because rain is a major source of sustenance and is itself sent in the measure God knows. | mentions 42:27
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p95/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The imperfect verb indicates repeated and renewed sending of rain; the past tense in after they despaired shows their despair had occurred and endured for some time.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p95/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The pronoun in after they despaired refers to God's servants mentioned in verse 25. | mentions 42:25
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p95/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · قيل | reports | One account says the verse followed the lifting of a seven-year drought in Mecca through the Prophet's prayer; Quraysh had eaten carrion and bones, and the episode is alluded to in 44:15. | mentions 44:15
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p95/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ghayth is rain that comes after drought; its name derives from the relief it brings to people in distress. | mentions 12:49
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p95/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Qunut means despair. | mentions 15:55
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p95/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | They despaired of rain when the usual signs of rain disappeared and the planting season was running out.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p95/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The restrictive construction is a reversal of the assumption that rain is governed by stars: it directly counters polytheists and treats inattentive Muslims as if they relied on customary causes.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p95/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · زيد بن خالد الجهني عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | After a night rain, the Prophet said people were divided: attributing rain to God's grace is faith in God and disbelief in stars, while attributing it to a star's phase reverses that allegiance.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p95/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Nashr is the opposite of folding and is used metaphorically here for expansion and extension. | mentions 17:13
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p95/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Mercy here means God's mercy through water.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p95/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · قيل | reports | Another interpretation takes the mercy to mean sunlight after the rain.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p96/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · عبد الله بن مسعود | reports | Al-Ṣaḥīḥ reports through Ibn Masud that after Quraysh rejected him, the Prophet prayed for seven years like Joseph; Abu Sufyan then pleaded for relief, and the Prophet prayed, warning they would relapse.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p96/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | The author says the event occurred in Medina and cites a report that the verse was revealed when a Bedouin asked the Prophet for rain during the Friday sermon.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p96/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · كعب بن مرة | reports | One version identifies the person who addressed the Prophet during the rain appeal as Kaʿb ibn Murra.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p96/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | reports | Another version in al-Ṣaḥīḥ has the Prophet pray against Quraysh and ask that they endure years like Joseph's years.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p96/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · نافع وابن عامر وعاصم وأبو جعفر | reports | These readers pronounce ينزل with fatḥa on the nūn and a doubled zāy; the remaining readers have sukūn on the nūn and a light zāy.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p96/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The paired attributes suit deliverance: the protecting ally does good to those under his care, and the praiseworthy giver grants what merits praise.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p96/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ḥamīd has the intensive adjective form faʿīl with passive meaning, mafʿūl.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p96/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · المهدوي | reports | Al-Mahdawī explains the spreading of mercy as the sun appearing after rain.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v25p96/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Rain is both a blessing and a sign of God's wondrous making and power, so the discourse digresses to signs affirming that God alone is divine.
[TABATABAI:42:28-29/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Qanūṭ means despair, and ghayth means rain.
[TABATABAI:42:28-29/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · مجمع البيان | reports | Majmaʿ al-Bayān distinguishes ghayth as rain beneficial in its season, while maṭar can be beneficial or harmful, in or out of season.
[TABATABAI:42:28-29/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Spreading mercy means distributing blessings through the growth of plants and production of fruit caused by rain.
[TABATABAI:42:28-29/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The discussion shifts from provision to signs of divine unity connected with provision, and further signs follow.
[TABATABAI:42:28-29/r8] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The closing names al-Walī and al-Ḥamīd praise God for His beautiful action.
[ASAD-NOTES:42:28#n32/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | The life-giving rain image connects to the preceding statement that God bestows grace in due measure. | mentions 42:27
[ASAD-NOTES:42:28#n32/r2] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | The rain reference prepares for the next verse's account of creation as a sign of God's existence and purposeful activity, and of life's continuation in the hereafter. | mentions 42:29
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p144/r2] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | God sends rain when people despair; because livelihood depends on it, this reminds them that neither deities nor human means control their provision.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p144/r3] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Rain is an everyday sign that God alone is the true accomplisher and al-Ḥamīd, worthy of good attributes, praise, and gratitude.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-7-english:p145/r1] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | God continues to sustain people through worldly life even when they challenge Him despite living on His provision.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:42:28/r1] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | God sends rain after people have lost hope, spreads His mercy, and is the true protector and worthy of all praise.
[QIRAAT-ER:42:28:4#1/r1] QIRAAT-ER · author | holds | The standard Form II with shadda marks repeated, intensified, or staged causative descent of rain.
[QIRAAT-ER:42:28:4#2/r1] QIRAAT-ER · author | holds | Form IV without shadda presents the rain’s descent as caused sending-down with less overt staging force.
[SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r2#2/f2] SAMARRAI-ASRAR · author | holds | The Quran uses amṭara for punitive rain but ghayth for good: 42:28 brings mercy after despair, and 12:49 describes a year of relief and harvest. | mentions 27:58, 26:173, 7:84, 25:40
[STUDYQURAN:42:28/r1] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | God sends rain when people have despaired, at their time of need, and spreads it over those in the region. | mentions 30:49, 41:39
[STUDYQURAN:42:28/r2] STUDYQURAN · Aj | reports | Spiritually, divine inspirations revive dead hearts through remembrance and knowledge after despair.
[STUDYQURAN:42:intro/r11] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | God is Provider and Sustainer, owns the keys of heaven and earth, and distributes provision by wisdom; this applies to wealth, offspring, and revelation.
